page: Microsoft Azure E16-4as_v4 is an EASv4-family virtual machine configured with 4 dedicated vCPUs and 128.0 GB of RAM. Powered by an AMD EPYC 7452 processor running at 3.35 GHz, the server features 2 physical cores with 2 threads per core on the x86_64 architecture. The CPU cache configuration includes 32 KB of L1d cache, 0.5 MB of L2 cache, and 16 MB of L3 cache. It is equipped with 262 GB of local storage, supports Premium Storage, and runs on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. No GPUs are included on this instance.

Benchmark data reveals a clear tradeoff between massive memory capacity and processing throughput. While the server achieves average performance in Geekbench single-core testing (1362.0) and large-block read-only memory bandwidth (45.48 GB/sec), its overall compute capabilities are limited. Multi-core CPU performance under stress-ng is categorized in the bottom 10%, and Passmark CPU scores are weak. Similarly, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and database operations on Passmark fall into the lower tiers, reflecting the constraints of having only 4 vCPUs paired with a massive memory footprint.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the E16-4as_v4 offers high memory density per vCPU, making it a specialized resource for memory-bound workloads that do not require intense parallel processing. The high RAM-to-vCPU ratio of 32 GB per core is well-suited for large in-memory caching, lightweight database hosting, and memory-intensive enterprise applications. However, it is not recommended for compute-heavy tasks, high-throughput web serving, or parallelized data processing due to its low multi-core benchmark results.
description: The Microsoft Azure E16-4as_v4 is an EASv4-family virtual machine optimized for memory-intensive workloads. It features 4 dedicated vCPUs powered by an AMD EPYC 7452 processor operating at 3.35 GHz, paired with a substantial 128.0 GB of RAM and 262 GB of local storage. Operating on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor, this instance provides a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 32 GB per core. Benchmark results highlight a significant tradeoff: while single-core Geekbench and large-block memory read bandwidth perform at average levels, multi-core CPU performance and database operations are weak. Consequently, this server is qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound applications that require large memory footprints without heavy parallel processing demands. It is best suited for in-memory caching, lightweight databases, and memory-heavy enterprise applications.
